```{r setup}
library(BayesianBenter)
set.seed(1)
```

## The Benter model

The Benter model (1994) is a generalization of the Plackett-Luce model for
rankings. A ranking is built sequentially: at stage $r$ the next item is
drawn from those still available with probability proportional to
$\lambda_j^{\alpha_r}$, where $\lambda_j > 0$ is an item's *worth* and
$\alpha_r \in (0, 1]$ is a stage-specific *dampening* (noise) exponent. Setting 
all $\alpha_r = 1$ recovers Plackett-Luce; smaller $\alpha_r$ flattens the 
choice probabilities, encoding the idea that rankers discriminate less sharply 
at later stages.

For identifiability we fix $\alpha_1 = 1$ and report the worths on the
sum-to-one scale.

## Simulate some rankings

```{r simulate}
lambda <- c(5, 3, 2, 1.5, 1)
lambda <- lambda / sum(lambda)
alpha  <- c(1, 0.8, 0.5, 0.3)   # length J - 1, alpha[1] = 1

pi <- rBenter(500, lambda, alpha)
head(pi)
```

## Fit the model

`gibbsBenter()` is the single entry point. Supply the data `pi`, the number of
items `J`, the Gamma(`a`, `b`) prior on the worths, and the Beta(`c`, `d`)
prior on the dampening exponents.

```{r fit}
fit <- gibbsBenter(pi, J = 5, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, d = 1,
                   iters = 2000, burnin = 0.5)

rbind(truth = lambda, posterior_mean = colMeans(fit$lambda))
rbind(truth = alpha,  posterior_mean = colMeans(fit$alpha))
```

The returned object stores the posterior draws (`fit$lambda`, `fit$alpha`) plus
sampler diagnostics in `fit$parameters`.

```{r trace, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3}
op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
matplot(fit$lambda, type = "l", lty = 1, xlab = "iteration", ylab = expression(lambda))
matplot(fit$alpha[, -1], type = "l", lty = 1, xlab = "iteration", ylab = expression(alpha))
par(op)
```

## Partial rankings

Partial (top-$R$) rankings are handled by the same function: leave the
unranked positions as `NA` (or pass a matrix with fewer than `J` columns).

```{r partial}
pi_partial <- pi
pi_partial[, 4:5] <- NA        # keep only the top 3 of each ranking
fit_p <- gibbsBenter(pi_partial, J = 5, a = 1, b = 1, c = 1, d = 1,
                     iters = 1000, burnin = 0.5)

# only dampening parameters up to the deepest observed rank are estimated
colMeans(fit_p$alpha)
fit_p$parameters$R_obs
```

Here only the top 3 items are observed, so `alpha_4` is not identified and is
returned as `NA`; the item worths for all five items are still estimated.

## A note on interval calibration

Credible intervals from this sampler are Bayesian, and their frequentist
coverage is only guaranteed asymptotically. In finite samples with many items,
short rankings, or widely-separated worths, coverage can fall below nominal
because the induced Dirichlet prior on the normalized worths is informative
(its strength grows with `J`) and because extreme worths sit near the boundary
of the simplex. Reducing `a` toward or below 1 lessens the prior's influence on
the normalized weights; checking coverage on a log-worth scale is often better
calibrated near the boundary.
